analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage sharply and then indexes it to inflation.
analysis.headline: A bill to raise the minimum wage from $5.15 to $8.15 over two years never got a House vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have raised the federal minimum wage from $5.15 to $6.65 an hour in 2002 and $8.15 in 2003 — roughly what the minimum wage bought in 1968 after adjusting for inflation — and tied future increases to the cost of living so it would stop eroding. It was introduced by Independent Rep. Bernard Sanders with 24 Democratic cosponsors, sent to the House Education and the Workforce Committee, then parked in a subcommittee, and never received a vote before the 107th Congress ended. [S2] [S3] [S4] [S5]
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly millions of workers earning the $5.15 federal minimum wage or close to it, concentrated in retail, restaurants, and other service jobs. The bill's findings state the minimum wage had lost 37% of its purchasing power since 1968, so the increase would directly raise paychecks at the bottom of the wage scale, and indexing to the cost of living would keep those raises from being eroded by inflation in later years. [S3]
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers earning minimum wage or near it

how_it_helps.text: Raises the minimum wage in two steps: to $6.65 an hour in 2002 and $8.15 in 2003, up from $5.15 — a 58% cumulative increase aimed at restoring the purchasing power the wage had at its 1968 peak. [S2] [S3]

Beginning in 2004, automatically adjusts the minimum wage each year using the same cost-of-living formula applied to Social Security benefits, so Congress would no longer have to act for the wage to keep pace with prices. [S2] [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Businesses that employ low-wage labor — restaurants, retail, agriculture, and small service firms — would bear higher payroll costs, and some of the increase would likely be passed to customers through prices. The bill's sharp two-step increase, arriving just months after passage, would fall hardest on small operators with thin margins and wage-heavy payrolls. [S3]

drawbacks.text: The increase is steep and fast: a 29% jump in 2002 followed by another 23% in 2003, with no regional adjustment for lower-cost areas. Small businesses with wage-heavy payrolls would face a sudden cost shock, and opponents of minimum wage increases generally argue some employers respond by cutting hours, entry-level positions, or hiring. [S3]

The indexation begins in 2004 with no off-ramp: the wage would rise automatically with inflation even in a recession, when lawmakers otherwise might freeze it to protect struggling employers. That automatic feature is exactly what supporters wanted, but it removes flexibility an honest supporter would acknowledge as a real trade-off. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the workers covered, the benefit is direct and large — pay at the bottom of the scale rising by more than half over two years, then protected from inflation. The cost is real but narrower: higher payroll costs for a segment of employers, with some pass-through to prices and some risk of reduced hours for the least-experienced workers. A slower phase-in or regional adjustment would have blunted the main objection, but as written the trade-off tilts clearly toward low-wage workers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and then to its Workforce Protections subcommittee, and no committee or floor vote ever happened before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bernard Sanders introduced the Minimum Wage Restoration Act on August 2, 2001, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce. [S5]
The bill would have raised the minimum wage from $5.15 to $6.65 in 2002 and $8.15 in 2003, then indexed it to the cost of living from 2004 onward. [S2] [S3]

On November 13, 2001, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections — a step that moved it out of the full committee's queue and into a smaller panel with no deadline to act. [S5]
The action record shows no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote at any point; the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003, with the bill still stalled in subcommittee. [S5]
Support was confined to the bill's Independent sponsor and 24 of the chamber's 208 House Democrats; no Republican cosponsored it. [S4]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers of minimum-wage labor — especially restaurants, retail, and other service businesses — were better off because the bill died: they continued paying the $5.15 wage, whose real value the bill itself documented as 37% below its 1968 level. Nothing changed for the workers the bill was written for. [S3] [S5]

for.name: Rep. Bernard Sanders
for.role: Independent Representative from Vermont; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Minimum Wage Restoration Act and recruited 24 Democratic cosponsors for it.

for.name: 24 of 208 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including the 16 members who signed on as original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: Rep. John Boehner
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: The committee he chaired never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill, and it was instead routed to a subcommittee with no action taken.

against.name: Speaker Dennis Hastert
against.what_they_did: The bill was never brought to the House floor for a vote during the 107th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Support came only from the Independent sponsor and 24 House Democrats — no Republican cosponsored the bill — and with Republicans holding 223 House seats, the legislation never had a path to a vote. [S4]

industries.note: Food service is the largest employer of minimum-wage workers, so the two-step increase to $8.15 would have hit its payroll costs hardest. The industry's interest in keeping the $5.15 wage runs directly against the pay raise the bill offered its own workers. [S2] [S3]

industries.industry: Retail and other low-wage service employers
industries.note: Retail, agriculture, and small service firms paying near $5.15 would have absorbed significant new labor costs under the bill's schedule. Their gain from the bill's death was the continued gap between the minimum wage and its 1968 buying power documented in the bill itself. [S3]
